lessons.title: Force diagrams, models and Newton's third law
lessons.summary: Isolate a particle, identify external forces, use model assumptions and apply Newton’s third law.
lessons.objective: Isolate a particle, identify external forces, use model assumptions and apply Newton’s third law.
lessons.before: Sketch the forces and choose positive directions before writing equations.
lessons.ideas:
A taut string pulls along the string, away from the particle. A rigid strut in compression pushes along the strut. Weight acts vertically downwards, while contact can exert a normal reaction and friction.

Use kilograms for \(m\), metres per second squared for \(g\), and newtons for \(W\). Use the value of \(g\) stated in the question.

Normal means perpendicular to the surface, including when it is sloping. A rough surface can have zero friction if no tangential resistance is needed.

If \(A\) pushes \(B\) with a particular force, \(B\) pushes \(A\) with the same magnitude and an opposite direction.

On one axis write \(\sum F=0\), with opposite senses given opposite signs.
lessons.method:
1. Choose the body first. For each arrow, name the external agent that exerts the force and its effect on the chosen body. A particle diagram uses a single point for the body.

  2. Mass measures how much matter is in the particle. Weight is the gravitational force on it. The equation \(W=mg\) converts a mass and local gravitational acceleration into a force.

  3. A smooth surface supplies no tangential force. It can still prevent penetration by exerting a normal reaction. A rough contact may also exert a force parallel to the surface.

  4. Each interaction involves two bodies. The force one exerts on the other has an equal and opposite partner of the same kind. The pair appears on two different free-body diagrams.

  5. In equilibrium the resultant force is zero. With forces along one axis, choose a positive direction, then add the signed forces. A body at rest or moving with constant velocity can be in equilibrium.
mistakes: Do not put both bodies' forces on one particle diagram. Forces exerted by the chosen particle on its surroundings belong elsewhere.
An arrow labelled just with the mass in kilograms is missing the factor \(g\).
Do not invent a friction arrow simply because a floor is rough. Inspect the other forces first.
Weight and normal reaction may be equal in a particular equilibrium, but both act on the same body and have different agents.
Zero velocity at an instant is insufficient evidence of equilibrium. The body must remain at rest or move with constant velocity.

examples.title: Select the forces on one body
examples.question: Isolate the beacon. It is suspended at rest from a vertical string. There is no other contact. Which list gives the forces acting on it?
examples.solution:
The Earth and the taut string are the only agents exerting forces on the beacon.

The force list is: weight and upward tension.

examples.title: Convert mass to weight
examples.question: Find the weight of a \(\frac{7}{4}\,\mathrm{kg}\) measuring unit. Take \(g=10\) metres per second squared.
examples.solution:
Mass measures the amount of matter. Weight is the gravitational force and acts vertically downwards.

Multiply the mass by the gravitational acceleration. \(W=\frac{7}{4}\times10=\frac{35}{2}\).

The weight is \(\frac{35}{2}\,\mathrm N\) vertically downwards.

examples.title: Convert mass to weight
examples.question: Find the weight of a \(\frac{3}{2}\,\mathrm{kg}\) sample carrier. Take \(g=\frac{49}{5}\) metres per second squared.
examples.solution:
Mass measures the amount of matter. Weight is the gravitational force and acts vertically downwards.

Multiply the mass by the gravitational acceleration. \(W=\frac{3}{2}\times\frac{49}{5}=\frac{147}{10}\).

The weight is \(\frac{147}{10}\,\mathrm N\) vertically downwards.

examples.title: Read the smooth-contact assumption
examples.question: A display panel is in contact with a smooth incline. What does the model imply about the contact force?
examples.solution:
A smooth contact has no friction component parallel to the surface.

The normal reaction is still present when the surface is pressing on the body. It points perpendicular to the surface.

lessons.title: Resolving forces and finding resultants
lessons.summary: Resolve signed components, combine forces and calculate the direction of a resultant or balancing force.
lessons.objective: Resolve signed components, combine forces and calculate the direction of a resultant or balancing force.
lessons.before: Sketch the forces and choose positive directions before writing equations.
lessons.ideas:
The reference determines the trig function. Cosine accompanies the stated reference axis, whether it is horizontal, vertical or tilted.

A negative component means it points against the corresponding positive axis. The magnitude of the full force remains non-negative.

Find \(S_x\) and \(S_y\) first. The magnitude is \(\sqrt{S_x^2+S_y^2}\).

When the horizontal component is non-zero, the reference angle to a horizontal ray has tangent \(\frac{|S_y|}{|S_x|}\). State above or below and right or left explicitly.

The balancing components are \(-S_x\) and \(-S_y\). Test that adding the new force gives zero on each axis.
lessons.method:
1. Draw the angle between the force arrow and the reference direction. The adjacent component has magnitude \(P\cos\theta\), while the opposite component has magnitude \(P\sin\theta\). Apply directional signs afterwards.

  2. Choose positive directions before resolving. An angle used in a right triangle gives positive side lengths, so those lengths need signs to show direction.

  3. Resolve each force along the same pair of perpendicular axes. Add rightwards components to obtain the horizontal total and upwards components to obtain the vertical total.

  4. The component signs identify the quadrant. Use the right triangle of component magnitudes to calculate an acute reference angle, then identify which axis and side that angle describes.

  5. An added force produces equilibrium when it cancels the existing resultant on both axes. It has the same magnitude as the resultant and points in the opposite direction.
mistakes: Do not automatically use cosine for horizontal. Check which line the angle is measured from.
Adding positive side lengths without checking directions can change both the resultant size and its direction.
Adding magnitudes gives an incorrect resultant unless all force arrows point in the same direction.
A number followed by a degree symbol is incomplete if the reference ray is not clear.
Reversing just one component generally reflects the arrow instead of reversing it.

examples.title: Resolve an angled force
examples.question: A force of \(25\,\mathrm N\) acts at angle \(\theta\) above the horizontal to the right. The acute angle \(\theta\) satisfies \(\tan \theta=\frac{3}{4}\). Take rightwards and upwards as positive. Find both signed components.
examples.solution:
The axis from which the angle is measured gives the adjacent side, so it uses cosine. The other uses sine.

\(\cos\theta=\frac{4}{5}\) and \(\sin\theta=\frac{3}{5}\). Apply the signs from the force direction.

The rightwards component is \(20\,\mathrm N\) and the upwards component is \(15\,\mathrm N\). Their expressions are \(25\cos\theta\) and \(25\sin\theta\).

examples.title: Resolve an angled force
examples.question: A force of \(50\,\mathrm N\) acts at angle \(\theta\) below the horizontal to the left. The acute angle \(\theta\) satisfies \(\tan \theta=\frac{3}{4}\). Take rightwards and upwards as positive. Find both signed components.
examples.solution:
The axis from which the angle is measured gives the adjacent side, so it uses cosine. The other uses sine.

\(\cos\theta=\frac{4}{5}\) and \(\sin\theta=\frac{3}{5}\). Apply the signs from the force direction.

The rightwards component is \(-40\,\mathrm N\) and the upwards component is \(-30\,\mathrm N\). Their expressions are \(-50\cos\theta\) and \(-50\sin\theta\).

examples.title: Resolve an angled force
examples.question: A force of \(63\,\mathrm N\) acts at angle \(\theta\) towards the left of the upward vertical. The acute angle \(\theta\) satisfies \(\tan \theta=\frac{12}{5}\). Take rightwards and upwards as positive. Find both signed components.
examples.solution:
The axis from which the angle is measured gives the adjacent side, so it uses cosine. The other uses sine.

\(\cos\theta=\frac{5}{13}\) and \(\sin\theta=\frac{12}{13}\). Apply the signs from the force direction.

The rightwards component is \(- \frac{756}{13}\,\mathrm N\) and the upwards component is \(\frac{315}{13}\,\mathrm N\). Their expressions are \(-63\sin\theta\) and \(63\cos\theta\).

examples.title: Find a resultant or balancing force
examples.question: Two forces act on a survey marker modelled as a particle. Their signed components are \(14\,\mathrm N\) rightwards and \(5\,\mathrm N\) upwards for the first, and \(-8\,\mathrm N\) rightwards and \(3\,\mathrm N\) upwards for the second. Find the rightwards and upwards components of the resultant, and its exact magnitude.
examples.solution:
\(S_x=14+\left(-8\right)=6\) and \(S_y=5+\left(3\right)=8\).

The magnitude follows from Pythagoras using the two resultant components.

The signed components are \(6\,\mathrm N\) rightwards and \(8\,\mathrm N\) upwards. The magnitude is \(10\,\mathrm N\).

lessons.title: Smooth equilibrium, inclines and tension
lessons.summary: Balance smooth contacts and strings in two directions, including an oblique pull and a suspended junction.
lessons.objective: Balance smooth contacts and strings in two directions, including an oblique pull and a suspended junction.
lessons.before: Sketch the forces and choose positive directions before writing equations.
lessons.ideas:
For inclination \(\alpha\), the weight component down the plane is \(W\sin\alpha\), and the component into the plane is \(W\cos\alpha\).

Resolve uphill for \(T=W\sin\alpha\) and away from the plane for \(R=W\cos\alpha\) in this particular model.

When the pull is horizontal, the equations are \(T\cos\alpha=W\sin\alpha\) and \(R=W\cos\alpha+T\sin\alpha\).

If tension makes angle \(\beta\) above the slope, then \(T\cos\beta=W\sin\alpha\) and \(R+T\sin\beta=W\cos\alpha\).

The two horizontal components cancel. The two upward components add to the load.
lessons.method:
1. Use one axis up the line of greatest slope and the other normal to the plane. Weight remains vertical in the diagram. The two component magnitudes come from the angle between vertical and the inward normal.

  2. On a smooth plane the tension can balance the downhill component of weight. If the string is parallel to the plane it has no normal component and only weight presses into the plane.

  3. An uphill horizontal pull makes angle \(\alpha\) with the slope. Its tangential part points uphill and its normal part presses the particle into the plane.

  4. A string directed above the slope has an outward component. Use the angle between string and slope, which can differ from the angle of the slope itself.

  5. Take the junction as the particle. The strings pull up and away from it, and the vertical load pulls down. Angles can differ, so the tensions need not match.
mistakes: The incline is not inclined relative to the weight direction by \(\alpha\). Look for the angle between the weight and the inward normal.
These equations assume the string is parallel to the plane. A tilted string changes both balance equations.
An uphill horizontal pull does not lift the particle away from an incline. Draw its normal component pointing inwards.
A surface cannot pull the particle towards itself. If your normal reaction would be negative, the assumed contact model fails.
A light junction contributes negligible weight of its own, but the stated load still acts on it.

examples.title: Resolve weight on a slope
examples.question: A particle has weight \(45\,\mathrm N\). A plane makes angle \(\alpha\) to the horizontal. The acute angle \(\alpha\) satisfies \(\tan \alpha=\frac{3}{4}\). Find the two magnitudes of the weight components downhill and into the plane.
examples.solution:
The weight points vertically downwards. Its angle to the inward normal is \(\alpha\).

The weight component along that normal is adjacent to the angle, so it uses cosine.

The downhill component is \(W\sin\alpha=27\) newtons and the inward component is \(W\cos\alpha=36\) newtons.

examples.title: Balance a particle on a smooth incline
examples.question: A particle of weight \(85\,\mathrm N\) rests on a smooth plane inclined at \(\alpha\) to the horizontal. A string pulls up the line of greatest slope, parallel to the incline. The acute angle \(\alpha\) satisfies \(\tan \alpha=\frac{3}{4}\). Find the tension and normal reaction.
examples.solution:
The weight has a downhill component \(51\,\mathrm N\) and a component \(68\,\mathrm N\) into the plane. Smooth contact gives no friction.

Tension is along the plane, so it has no normal component.

Resolve uphill. \(1T=51\) gives \(T=51\).

Resolve outwards. \(R+\left(0\right)T=68\) gives \(R=68\).

The tension is \(51\,\mathrm N\) and the normal reaction is \(68\,\mathrm N\).

examples.title: Balance a particle on a smooth incline
examples.question: A particle of weight \(102\,\mathrm N\) rests on a smooth plane inclined at \(\alpha\) to the horizontal. A string pulls up the line of greatest slope, parallel to the incline. The acute angle \(\alpha\) satisfies \(\tan \alpha=\frac{8}{15}\). Find the tension and normal reaction.
examples.solution:
The weight has a downhill component \(48\,\mathrm N\) and a component \(90\,\mathrm N\) into the plane. Smooth contact gives no friction.

Tension is along the plane, so it has no normal component.

Resolve uphill. \(1T=48\) gives \(T=48\).

Resolve outwards. \(R+\left(0\right)T=90\) gives \(R=90\).

The tension is \(48\,\mathrm N\) and the normal reaction is \(90\,\mathrm N\).

examples.title: Balance a particle on a smooth incline
examples.question: A particle of weight \(48\,\mathrm N\) rests on a smooth plane inclined at \(\alpha\) to the horizontal. A string pulls horizontally towards the higher side of the plane. The acute angle \(\alpha\) satisfies \(\tan \alpha=\frac{4}{3}\). Find the tension and normal reaction.
examples.solution:
The weight has a downhill component \(\frac{192}{5}\,\mathrm N\) and a component \(\frac{144}{5}\,\mathrm N\) into the plane. Smooth contact gives no friction.

The horizontal tension resolves to \(T\cos\alpha\) uphill and \(T\sin\alpha\) into the incline.

Resolve uphill. \(\frac{3}{5}T=\frac{192}{5}\) gives \(T=64\).

Resolve outwards. \(R+\left(- \frac{4}{5}\right)T=\frac{144}{5}\) gives \(R=80\).

The tension is \(64\,\mathrm N\) and the normal reaction is \(80\,\mathrm N\).

lessons.title: Rough equilibrium and limiting friction
lessons.summary: Find signed friction from equilibrium, check its limit and combine the two components of contact.
lessons.objective: Find signed friction from equilibrium, check its limit and combine the two components of contact.
lessons.before: Sketch the forces and choose positive directions before writing equations.
lessons.ideas:
At rest, determine the friction from \(\sum F_{\parallel}=0\). Then test \(|f|\le\mu R\), where \(f\) denotes signed friction.

‘On the point of sliding’ or ‘about to slip’ indicates \(F=\mu R\), where \(F=|f|\).

With uphill positive, \(f=W\sin\alpha-P_{\parallel}\). Positive \(f\) acts uphill, negative \(f\) downhill, and \(f=0\) indicates no friction.

On a horizontal floor, an upward force component \(P_y\) gives \(R=W-P_y\). A signed negative \(P_y\) makes the reaction larger than \(W\).

The two contact components are perpendicular, so total contact-force magnitude is \(\sqrt{R^2+f^2}\).
lessons.method:
1. First find the force that would unbalance the particle along the surface if friction were absent. Static friction supplies the opposite force if it lies within the available limit.

  2. A resting particle is in limiting equilibrium when the friction required just equals the maximum possible magnitude. Any extra demand in the same direction would break the balance.

  3. Weight alone tends to pull a particle down the slope, but an applied force may exceed that effect. To find friction, compare the tangential force components before including friction.

  4. An oblique pull can reduce the normal reaction by partly supporting the weight. A push into the surface can increase it. The friction limit changes with the reaction.

  5. The phrase normal reaction refers only to the component perpendicular to the surface. The full contact force is the vector sum of the normal reaction and friction.
mistakes: Using \(F=\mu R\) in every question can invent an unbalanced force on a particle already at rest.
A value beyond the limit is a sign that there is no equilibrium. Do not report the required balance force as actual friction when it is unavailable.
Friction does not automatically act uphill, and there may be no static friction despite rough contact.
The reaction does not automatically equal the weight. Resolve across the surface before multiplying by \(\mu\).
Use the friction found from equilibrium. Do not replace it with the maximum unless the particle is at the limit.

examples.title: Resolve before using the friction limit
examples.question: A particle of weight \(86\,\mathrm N\) is on a rough horizontal floor. A force of \(14\,\mathrm N\) acts to the right, parallel to the floor. The coefficient of friction is \(\frac{1}{2}\). Find the normal reaction, the friction magnitude required for equilibrium and the maximum friction. Decide whether the particle can be in equilibrium.
examples.solution:
Take rightwards and upwards as positive. Resolve the applied force: \(14\,\mathrm N\) rightwards and \(0\,\mathrm N\) upwards.

Vertical equilibrium gives \(R=86\). Then \(\mu R=43\).

The required friction is less than the maximum. The floor supplies the required friction to the left.

The normal reaction is \(86\,\mathrm N\), required friction is \(14\,\mathrm N\), and the maximum is \(43\,\mathrm N\). The floor supplies the required friction to the left.

examples.title: Compare required and available friction
examples.question: A particle of weight \(50\,\mathrm N\) is on a rough plane inclined at angle \(\alpha\) to the horizontal. A force of \(10\,\mathrm N\) acts up the line of greatest slope, parallel to the incline. The acute angle \(\alpha\) satisfies \(\tan \alpha=\frac{3}{4}\). The coefficient of friction is \(\frac{1}{2}\). With uphill positive, find the signed friction that equilibrium would require, the maximum friction, and the equilibrium status.
examples.solution:
Take uphill and outwards as positive. Normal balance gives \(R=40-\left(0\right)=40\).

With signed friction \(f\) uphill positive, tangential balance gives \(f=30-10=20\).

The required friction has magnitude \(20\,\mathrm N\) and would act uphill.

The maximum is \(\mu R=\frac{1}{2}\times 40=20\).

Required signed friction is \(20\,\mathrm N\), and the maximum is \(20\,\mathrm N\). The particle is in limiting equilibrium. Friction is at its available limit.

examples.title: Compare required and available friction
examples.question: A particle of weight \(68\,\mathrm N\) is on a rough plane inclined at angle \(\alpha\) to the horizontal. A force of \(15\,\mathrm N\) acts up the line of greatest slope, parallel to the incline. The acute angle \(\alpha\) satisfies \(\tan \alpha=\frac{8}{15}\). The coefficient of friction is \(\frac{1}{4}\). With uphill positive, find the signed friction that equilibrium would require, the maximum friction, and the equilibrium status.
examples.solution:
Take uphill and outwards as positive. Normal balance gives \(R=60-\left(0\right)=60\).

With signed friction \(f\) uphill positive, tangential balance gives \(f=32-15=17\).

The required friction has magnitude \(17\,\mathrm N\) and would act uphill.

The maximum is \(\mu R=\frac{1}{4}\times 60=15\).

Required signed friction is \(17\,\mathrm N\), and the maximum is \(15\,\mathrm N\). Equilibrium is impossible because the required friction exceeds the limit. The friction required by the balance equations is not an actual equilibrium force in this case.

examples.title: Compare required and available friction
examples.question: A particle of weight \(75\,\mathrm N\) is on a rough plane inclined at angle \(\alpha\) to the horizontal. A force of \(60\,\mathrm N\) acts up the line of greatest slope, parallel to the incline. The acute angle \(\alpha\) satisfies \(\tan \alpha=\frac{3}{4}\). The coefficient of friction is \(\frac{1}{2}\). With uphill positive, find the signed friction that equilibrium would require, the maximum friction, and the equilibrium status.
examples.solution:
Take uphill and outwards as positive. Normal balance gives \(R=60-\left(0\right)=60\).

With signed friction \(f\) uphill positive, tangential balance gives \(f=45-60=-15\).

The required friction has magnitude \(15\,\mathrm N\) and would act downhill.

The maximum is \(\mu R=\frac{1}{2}\times 60=30\).

Required signed friction is \(-15\,\mathrm N\), and the maximum is \(30\,\mathrm N\). Equilibrium is possible and is below the limiting condition.

lessons.title: Limiting cases and ranges of equilibrium
lessons.summary: Find a minimum coefficient, a maximum inclination and the full range of a holding force.
lessons.objective: Find a minimum coefficient, a maximum inclination and the full range of a holding force.
lessons.before: Sketch the forces and choose positive directions before writing equations.
lessons.ideas:
If \(R>0\), then \(\mu\ge\frac{|f|}{R}\). The right side is the minimum. The same expression equals the coefficient if the body is stated to be about to slip.

\(W\sin\alpha\le\mu W\cos\alpha\) leads to \(\tan\alpha\le\mu\) on \(0\le\alpha<90^\circ\).

For a parallel pull, \(-\mu W\cos\alpha\le W\sin\alpha-P\le\mu W\cos\alpha\). Intersect the result with \(P\ge0\).

Split into \(f\le\mu R\) and \(-f\le\mu R\). Solve each signed inequality, checking the sign of any coefficient you divide by.

A magnitude satisfies \(P\ge0\). Contact requires \(R\ge0\); if \(R=0\), the available friction is also zero.
lessons.method:
1. First calculate how much friction the forces demand and how strongly the particle presses on the plane. Then find the coefficient for which the available friction first meets that demand.

  2. With just weight and the reaction from the rough plane, equilibrium needs friction uphill. Check the ratio of the downhill weight component to the normal weight component.

  3. With an uphill pull, too little can let the particle slip down, while too much can make it tend to slip up. Keep one fixed positive direction so the same inequality detects both cases.

  4. Resolve normal to the surface to express \(R\) in terms of \(P\). Keep this expression in both sides of \(|f|\le\mu R\), and check contact across the proposed interval.

  5. A negative lower endpoint can mean that the given friction is already enough with no applied pull. Intersect the algebraic range with the physical possibilities.
mistakes: Use the magnitude of friction. A negative signed friction gives direction, not a negative coefficient.
The coefficient of friction is a ratio and has no units of angle. Use inverse tangent to find the angle in degrees.
Using only the downhill-slip boundary misses the upper limit. Both limiting end-values are allowed when static friction can reach the limit.
Do not use one constant value of \(R\) across the range when the pull has a normal component.
A negative answer for a magnitude is not a force pointing the other way unless the problem explicitly defines a signed force.

examples.title: Find the minimum coefficient of friction
examples.question: A particle of weight \(65\,\mathrm N\) is at rest on a rough plane inclined at \(\alpha\) to the horizontal. An applied force of \(58\,\mathrm N\) acts up the line of greatest slope, parallel to the incline. The acute angle \(\alpha\) satisfies \(\tan \alpha=\frac{3}{4}\). Find the least possible coefficient of friction.
examples.solution:
Resolve perpendicular to the plane to obtain \(R=52\). The applied force contributes \(0\,\mathrm N\) outwards.

Resolve along the plane to find the signed friction required. Using uphill as positive gives \(f=-19\). The friction is downhill.

For equilibrium \(|f|\le\mu R\). The minimum occurs when equality first becomes possible.

The least coefficient is \(\mu_{\min}=\frac{19}{52}=\frac{19}{52}\).

examples.title: Find the greatest angle for equilibrium
examples.question: A particle rests on a rough plane with no applied force other than its weight and the contact force. The coefficient of friction is \(\frac{2}{3}\). Find the greatest possible angle of the plane above the horizontal, to one decimal place.
examples.solution:
At inclination \(\alpha\) the uphill friction required is \(W\sin\alpha\) and the normal reaction is \(W\cos\alpha\).

Demand cannot exceed capacity, so \(\tan\alpha\le\mu\). On the acute interval tangent increases with the angle.

The limiting angle is \(\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)=33.7^\circ\).

examples.title: Find the greatest angle for equilibrium
examples.question: A particle rests on a rough plane with no applied force other than its weight and the contact force. The coefficient of friction is \(\frac{1}{3}\). Find the greatest possible angle of the plane above the horizontal, to one decimal place.
examples.solution:
At inclination \(\alpha\) the uphill friction required is \(W\sin\alpha\) and the normal reaction is \(W\cos\alpha\).

Demand cannot exceed capacity, so \(\tan\alpha\le\mu\). On the acute interval tangent increases with the angle.

The limiting angle is \(\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)=18.4^\circ\).

examples.title: Find both bounds for a holding force
examples.question: A particle of weight \(50\,\mathrm N\) is held in equilibrium on a rough plane inclined at \(\alpha\) to the horizontal. A force of magnitude \(P\) newtons acts up the line of greatest slope, parallel to the incline. The acute angle \(\alpha\) satisfies \(\tan \alpha=\frac{3}{4}\). The coefficient of friction is \(\frac{1}{4}\). Find the inclusive range of \(P\).
examples.solution:
Let signed friction \(f\) be positive uphill. Normal balance gives \(R=40\). Uphill balance gives \(f=30 - P\).

With contact maintained require \(R\ge0\) and \(-\mu R\le f\le\mu R\). Split the friction condition into two inequalities.

The downhill-slip boundary gives \(1P\ge 20\), so \(P\ge 20\).

The uphill-slip boundary gives \(1P\le 40\), so \(P\le 40\).

Combine the inequalities with \(P\ge0\) and the contact condition. The normal reaction is positive throughout \(20\le P\le 40\) (in newtons), including both endpoints.

Use the horizontal equation to write \(T_R=\frac{13}{20}T_L\). Substitute this into the vertical equation.

The left tension is \(\frac{800}{7}\,\mathrm N\) and the right tension is \(\frac{520}{7}\,\mathrm N\).

questions.title: Compare two ways of supporting the same particle
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of weight \(72\,\mathrm N\) is held on a smooth incline of acute angle \(\alpha\) to the horizontal, where \(\tan\alpha=\frac5{12}\).

  1. A string parallel to the incline holds the particle. Find its tension and the normal reaction. [3]

  2. The string is replaced by a horizontal string pulling towards the higher side. Find the new tension and reaction, and explain why the reaction has increased. [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a) The tension is \(\frac{360}{13}\,\mathrm N\) and the normal reaction is \(\frac{864}{13}\,\mathrm N\).

(b) The normal reaction increases to \(78\,\mathrm N\) because the horizontal tension also presses the particle into the plane.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The weight has a downhill component \(\frac{360}{13}\,\mathrm N\) and a component \(\frac{864}{13}\,\mathrm N\) into the plane. Smooth contact gives no friction.

Tension is along the plane, so it has no normal component.

Resolve uphill. \(1T=\frac{360}{13}\) gives \(T=\frac{360}{13}\).

Resolve outwards. \(R+\left(0\right)T=\frac{864}{13}\) gives \(R=\frac{864}{13}\).

The tension is \(\frac{360}{13}\,\mathrm N\) and the normal reaction is \(\frac{864}{13}\,\mathrm N\).

Part (b)

The weight has a downhill component \(\frac{360}{13}\,\mathrm N\) and a component \(\frac{864}{13}\,\mathrm N\) into the plane. Smooth contact gives no friction.

The horizontal tension resolves to \(T\cos\alpha\) uphill and \(T\sin\alpha\) into the incline.

Resolve uphill. \(\frac{12}{13}T=\frac{360}{13}\) gives \(T=30\).

Resolve outwards. \(R+\left(- \frac{5}{13}\right)T=\frac{864}{13}\) gives \(R=78\).

The tension is \(30\,\mathrm N\) and the normal reaction is \(78\,\mathrm N\).

The normal reaction increases to \(78\,\mathrm N\) because the horizontal tension also presses the particle into the plane.

A particle is held at rest on a smooth incline by a string parallel to the line of greatest slope. The tension is \(27\,\mathrm N\) and the reaction is \(36\,\mathrm N\).

The weight has a downhill component \(27\,\mathrm N\) and a component \(36\,\mathrm N\) into the plane. Smooth contact gives no friction.

The horizontal tension resolves to \(T\cos\alpha\) uphill and \(T\sin\alpha\) into the incline.

Resolve uphill. \(\frac{4}{5}T=27\) gives \(T=\frac{135}{4}\).

Resolve outwards. \(R+\left(- \frac{3}{5}\right)T=36\) gives \(R=\frac{225}{4}\).

The tension is \(\frac{135}{4}\,\mathrm N\) and the normal reaction is \(\frac{225}{4}\,\mathrm N\).

questions.prompt_html: A particle of weight \(65\,\mathrm N\) is held in equilibrium on a rough plane inclined at \(\alpha\) to the horizontal. A force of magnitude \(P\) newtons acts up the line of greatest slope, parallel to the incline. The acute angle \(\alpha\) satisfies \(\tan \alpha=\frac{3}{4}\). The coefficient of friction is \(\frac{1}{3}\). Find the inclusive range of \(P\).
questions.answer_html: Combine the inequalities with \(P\ge0\) and the contact condition. The normal reaction is positive throughout \(\frac{65}{3}\le P\le \frac{169}{3}\) (in newtons), including both endpoints.
questions.solution_html:
Let signed friction \(f\) be positive uphill. Normal balance gives \(R=52\). Uphill balance gives \(f=39 - P\).

With contact maintained require \(R\ge0\) and \(-\mu R\le f\le\mu R\). Split the friction condition into two inequalities.

The downhill-slip boundary gives \(1P\ge \frac{65}{3}\), so \(P\ge \frac{65}{3}\).

The uphill-slip boundary gives \(1P\le \frac{169}{3}\), so \(P\le \frac{169}{3}\).

Combine the inequalities with \(P\ge0\) and the contact condition. The normal reaction is positive throughout \(\frac{65}{3}\le P\le \frac{169}{3}\) (in newtons), including both endpoints.
questions.hint_html: Write a single signed expression for friction. Then use both sides of its limit inequality.

questions.title: Both limits of a rescue line
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of weight \(100\,\mathrm N\) is held on a rough incline, with \(\tan\alpha=\frac34\) and \(\mu=\frac14\). A rescue line pulls with force \(P\,\mathrm N\) uphill, parallel to the plane.

  1. Determine the complete range of \(P\) for equilibrium. [4]

  2. At each endpoint state the direction of impending slip. Find the force for which friction vanishes. [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a) Combine the inequalities with \(P\ge0\) and the contact condition. The normal reaction is positive throughout \(40\le P\le 80\) (in newtons), including both endpoints.

(b) Friction is zero when \(P=60\). The lower endpoint has impending downhill slip, and the upper endpoint has impending uphill slip.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Let signed friction \(f\) be positive uphill. Normal balance gives \(R=80\). Uphill balance gives \(f=60 - P\).

With contact maintained require \(R\ge0\) and \(-\mu R\le f\le\mu R\). Split the friction condition into two inequalities.

The downhill-slip boundary gives \(1P\ge 40\), so \(P\ge 40\).

The uphill-slip boundary gives \(1P\le 80\), so \(P\le 80\).

Combine the inequalities with \(P\ge0\) and the contact condition. The normal reaction is positive throughout \(40\le P\le 80\) (in newtons), including both endpoints.

Part (b)

The signed friction is \(60-P\). At \(P=40\) it acts uphill, so the impending slip is downhill. At \(P=80\) it acts downhill, so the impending slip is uphill.

Friction is zero when \(P=60\). The lower endpoint has impending downhill slip, and the upper endpoint has impending uphill slip.
questions.hint_html: Use one signed friction formula. At each limit its sign tells you the direction that friction acts.

questions.title: The steepest shelf
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of weight \(70\,\mathrm N\) rests on a rough tilting shelf. The coefficient of friction is \(\frac25\). No tether acts on the particle.

  1. Find the largest inclination for rest, to one decimal place. [3]

  2. The shelf is instead set to \(\tan\alpha=\frac13\). Determine whether limiting equilibrium occurs and calculate the least coefficient for which the particle could rest at this angle. [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a) The limiting angle is \(\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)\approx 21.8^\circ\).

(b) At \(\mu=\frac25\), the equilibrium is non-limiting. The least coefficient at this angle is \(\frac13\), for which the friction would be limiting.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

At inclination \(\alpha\) the uphill friction required is \(W\sin\alpha\) and the normal reaction is \(W\cos\alpha\).

Demand cannot exceed capacity, so \(\tan\alpha\le\mu\). On the acute interval tangent increases with the angle.

The limiting angle is \(\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)\approx 21.8^\circ\).

Part (b)

The demand divided by the reaction equals \(\tan\alpha=\frac13\). This is less than the actual coefficient \(\frac25\), so there is equilibrium below the limit.

The least coefficient at this angle is \(\frac13\), for which the friction would be limiting.
questions.hint_html: With no other applied force, the weight cancels from the inequality after using W sin α and W cos α.

questions.title: A horizontal pull that increases contact
questions.prompt_html:
A particle of weight \(50\,\mathrm N\) is held on a rough incline where \(\tan\alpha=\frac34\) and \(\mu=\frac14\). A horizontal pull of magnitude \(P\,\mathrm N\) acts towards the higher side of the incline.

  1. Write expressions for the normal reaction and signed uphill friction, in terms of \(P\). [3]

  2. Determine the exact range of \(P\) for which the particle can be at rest. [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a) Balance the normal components to obtain \(R=40+\frac35P\). Uphill balance gives \(f=30-\frac45P\).

(b) Combine the inequalities with \(P\ge0\) and the contact condition. The normal reaction is positive throughout \(\frac{400}{19}\le P\le \frac{800}{13}\) (in newtons), including both endpoints.
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

The horizontal force has component \(\frac45P\) up the plane and \(\frac35P\) into the plane.

Balance the normal components to obtain \(R=40+\frac35P\). Uphill balance gives \(f=30-\frac45P\).

Part (b)

Let signed friction \(f\) be positive uphill. Normal balance gives \(R=\frac{3 P}{5} + 40\). Uphill balance gives \(f=30 - \frac{4 P}{5}\).

With contact maintained require \(R\ge0\) and \(-\mu R\le f\le\mu R\). Split the friction condition into two inequalities.

The downhill-slip boundary gives \(\frac{19}{20}P\ge 20\), so \(P\ge \frac{400}{19}\).

The uphill-slip boundary gives \(\frac{13}{20}P\le 40\), so \(P\le \frac{800}{13}\).

Combine the inequalities with \(P\ge0\) and the contact condition. The normal reaction is positive throughout \(\frac{400}{19}\le P\le \frac{800}{13}\) (in newtons), including both endpoints.
questions.hint_html: The normal reaction is a function of P. Keep that function inside both inequalities.
